2 Graph Representation
• Given an adjacency-list representation of a graph G = (V, E), write an algorithm to obtain the adjacency-matrix
representation of G.
Algorithm 1 Adjacency-List-To-Adjacency-Matrix
Input: Adj-List[1, 2, . . . , |G.V |]: Adjacency-list representation of a graph G = (V, E)
Output: Adj-Matrix[1, 2, . . . , |G.V |][1, 2, . . . , |G.V |]: Adjacency-matrix representation of the graph G
1: n ← |G.V | . Number of vertices in G
2: m ← |G.E| . Number of edges in G
3: Create an adjacency matrix Adj-Matrix[1, 2, . . . , n][1, 2, . . . , n] of size n × n
4: for each vertex u ∈ G.V do
5: for each vertex v ∈ G.V do
6: Adj-Matrix[u][v] ← 0 . Initialize each element of the adjacency-matrix with 0
7: end for
8: end for
9: for each vertex u ∈ G.V do
10: for each vertex v ∈ Adj-List[u] do
11: Adj-Matrix[u][v] ← 1 . Edge from u to v
12: end for
13: end for
14: return Adj-Matrix

• Given an adjacency-matrix representation of a graph G = (V, E), write an algorithm to obtain the adjacency-list
representation of G.
Algorithm 2 Adjacency-Matrix-To-Adjacency-List
Input: Adj-Matrix[1, 2, . . . , |G.V |][1, 2, . . . , |G.V |]: Adjacency-matrix representation of a graph G = (V, E)
Output: Adj-List[1, 2, . . . , |G.V |]: Adjacency-list representation of the graph G
1: n ← |G.V | . Number of vertices in G
2: m ← |G.E| . Number of edges in G
3: Create an adjacency list Adj-List[1, 2, . . . , n] of size n
4: for each vertex u ∈ G.V do
5: Adj-List[u] ← ∅ . Initialize an empty adjacency-list for vertex u
6: end for
7: for each vertex u ∈ G.V do
8: for each vertex v ∈ G.V do
9: if Adj-Matrix[u][v] = 1 then . Check for an edge from u to v
10: Adj-List[u] ← Adj-List[u] ∪ {v} . Add v to the adjacency-list of u
11: end if
12: end for
13: end for
14: return Adj-List

3 Degree of Vertices in the Graph
• Given an adjacency-list representation of a directed graph G = (V, E), write an algorithm to obtain the in-degree
and out-degree of all the vertices.
Algorithm 3 In-Out-Degree-Directed-Graph-Adjecancy-List
Input: Adj-List[1, 2, . . . , |G.V |]: Adjacency-list representation of a directed graph G = (V, E)
Output: In-degree and out-degree of all the vertices in the graph G
1: n ← |G.V | . Number of vertices in G
2: m ← |G.E| . Number of edges in G
3: for each vertex u ∈ G.V do
4: u.in-degree ← 0 . Initialize in-degree of vertex u to be 0
5: u.out-degree ← 0 . Initialize out-degree of vertex u to be 0
6: end for
7: for each vertex u ∈ G.V do
8: u.out-degree ← |Adj-List[u]|
9: for each vertex v ∈ Adj-List[u] do
10: v.in-degree ← v.in-degree + 1
11: end for
12: end for
13: return in-degree and out-degree of vertices

5 Breadth-First Search (BFS)
Given a graph G = (V, E) and a source vertex s, breadth-first search systematically explores the edges of G to
“discover” every vertex that is reachable from s.
• It computes the distance from s to each reachable vertex, where the distance to a vertex v equals the smallest
number of edges needed to go from s to v.
• Breadth-first search produces a “breadth-first tree” with root s that contains all reachable vertices.
• For any vertex v reachable from s, the simple path in the breadth-first tree from s to v corresponds to a shortest
path from s to v in G.
• The algorithm works on both directed and undirected graphs.
Algorithm 9 BFS-Print(s, G)
1: for each vertex v ∈ V do
2: u.visited ← False . Vertex u is not visited initially
3: end for
4: Q ← ∅ . Create a queue to store the vertices
5: s.visited ← True . Mark source vertex s as visited
6: Q.Enqueue(s) . Insert source vertex s in the queue
7: while Q 6= ∅ do . Q is not empty
8: u ← Q.Dequeue() . Remove the vertex from the queue
9: for each vertex v ∈ G.Adj[u] do . Explore all the adjacent vertices of vertex u
10: if v.visited = False then . Vertex v is not visited
11: v.visited ← True . Mark vertex v as visited
12: Q.Enqueue(v) . Insert vertex v in the queue
13: end if
14: end for
15: end while

Algorithm 10 BFS-Distance(s, G)
1: for each vertex v ∈ V do
2: u.d ← ∞ . Number of edges to reach vertex u from source vertex s is ∞
3: u.π ← Nil . No predecessor of vertex u, so Nil
4: u.visited ← False . Vertex u is not visited initially
5: end for
6: Q ← ∅ . Create a queue to store the vertices
7: s.visited ← True . Mark source vertex s as visited
8: s.d ← 0 . Number of edges to reach vertex s from source s is 0
9: Q.Enqueue(s) . Insert source vertex s in the queue
10: while Q 6= ∅ do . Q is not empty
11: u ← Q.Dequeue() . Remove the vertex from the queue
12: for each vertex v ∈ G.Adj[u] do . Explore all the adjacent vertices of vertex u
13: if v.visited = False then . Vertex v is not visited
14: v.visited ← True . Mark vertex v as visited
15: v.π ← u . Make vertex u as a predecessor of vertex v
16: v.d ← u.d + 1 . Number of edges to reach vertex v from source vertex s
17: Q.Enqueue(v) . Insert vertex v in the queue
18: end if
19: end for
20: end while
Applications:
• Shortest path (considering the number of edges) from source vertex
• Diameter of a graph
– Undirected Graph: Maximum distance in any BFS ≤ Diameter ≤ 2×Maximum distance in any BFS
– Directed Graph: Diameter ≤ 2 × Maxim distance in any BFS
• Bipartite graph

Diameter of a graph: Given a graph (undirected/directed) G = (V, E) where the edge weight of all the edges
are equal. The diameter of this graph G is defined as the largest shortest path distance in the graph, i.e., diameter
= maxu,v∈V δ(u, v) where δ(u, v) is the shortest distance between vertices u and v.
Algorithm 11 Diameter
Input: Adj-List[1, 2, . . . , |G.V |]: Adjacency list representation of an undirected graph G = (V, E)
Output: Diameter of the graph G
1: n ← |G.V | . Number of vertices in G
2: m ← |G.E| . Number of edges in G
3: diameter ← −∞
4: for each vertex u ∈ G.V do
5: Apply BFS(u) and find the maximum distance label. Let this distance label be du.
6: if du > diameter then
7: diameter ← du
8: end if
9: end for
10: return diameter

Output: True: If the graph is bipartite, False: otherwise
1: n ← |G.V | . Number of vertices in G
2: m ← |G.E| . Number of edges in G
3: for each vertex u ∈ G.V do
4: u.color ← Nil
5: end for
6: s ← A random vertex from G.V . Select a source vertex randomly
7: s.color ← Red . Color source vertex s as Red
8: Q.Enqueue(s) . Add s to the queue
9: while Q 6= ∅ do
10: u ← Q.Dequeue() . Dequeue from Q
11: for each vertex v ∈ Adj-List[u] do
12: if v.color = Nil then . Vertex v is not colored
13: if u.color = Red then
14: v.color ← Blue . Color vertex v as Blue

23: end if

6 Depth-First Search (DFS)
Given a graph G = (V, E), depth-first search searches “deeper” in the graph whenever possible.
• Discovery and finish times obtained from DFS traversal have parenthesis structure.
• Depth-first search produces a “breadth-first forest”.
• The algorithm works on both directed and undirected graphs.
Algorithm 13 DFS-Iterative(s, G)
1: for each vertex v ∈ V do
2: u.visited ← False . Vertex u is not visited initially
3: end for
4: S ← ∅ . Create a stack to store the vertices
5: s.visited ← True . Mark source vertex s as visited
6: S.Push(s) . Push source vertex s into the stack
7: while S 6= ∅ do . S is not empty
8: u ← Q.Pop() . Pop the vertex from the stack
9: for each vertex v ∈ G.Adj[u] do . Explore all the adjacent vertices of vertex u
10: if v.visited = False then . Vertex v is not visited
11: v.visited ← True . Mark vertex v as visited
12: S.Push(v) . Push vertex v into the stack
13: end if
14: end for
15: end while
Algorithm 14 DFS-Recursive(s, G)
1: for each vertex v ∈ V do
2: u.visited ← False . Vertex u is not visited initially
3: end for
4: DFS-Visit(G, s)
Algorithm 15 DFS-Visit(u, G)
1: u.visited ← True . Mark vertex u as visited
2: for each vertex v ∈ G.Adj[u] do . Explore all the adjacent vertices of vertex u
3: if v.visited = False then . Vertex v is not visited
4: DFS-Visit(G, v)
5: end if
6: end for
Applications:
• Directed Graph
– Obtain the strongly connected components in a directed graph G = (V, E)
– Check whether a directed graph G = (V, E) contains a cycle or not?
– Topological sorting in a directed graph G = (V, E)
• Undirected Graph
– Check whether an undirected graph G = (V, E) contains a cycle or not?
– Given an undirected graph G = (V, E). Any edge whose removal results in a disconnected graph is known
as Bridge. A graph is 2-edge connected if it contains no bridges. Check whether the graph G is 2-edge

/* – – – – – Check for the bridges – – – – – */

1: time ← time + 1

4: u.low ← u.d . Initialize low

7 Connected Graph
• Given an undirected graph G = (V, E). Write an algorithm to check whether the graph G is connected or not.
Algorithm 19 Connected
Input: An undirected graph G = (V, E)
Output: True: If the graph is connected, False: otherwise
1: n ← |G.V | . Number of vertices in G
2: m ← |G.E| . Number of edges in G
3: for each vertex u ∈ G.V do
4: Lu ← DFS(u, G) . Apply DFS/BFS considering vertex u as a source
and store all the vertices reachable from u (including u) in Lu
5: if |Lu| < n then . All the vertices are not reachable from u
6: return False . Graph G is not connected
7: end if
8: end for
9: return True . Graph G is connected
Algorithm 20 Connected-Better
Input: An undirected graph G = (V, E)
Output: True: If the graph is connected, False: otherwise

and store all the vertices reachable from u (including u) in Lu
5: if |Lu| = n then . All the vertices are reachable from u
6: return True . Graph G is connected
7: else . All the vertices are not reachable from u
8: return False . Graph G is not connected
9: end if

8 Strongly Connected Components (SCCs)
Algorithm 24 SCC-Naive
Input: A directed graph G = (V, E)
Output: All the strongly connected components in the graph G
1: n ← |G.V | . Number of vertices in G
2: m ← |G.E| . Number of edges in G
3: for each vertex u ∈ G.V do
4: u.inSCC ← False . Vertex u is not the part of any SCC
5: end for
6: SCComponents ← ∅ . Initially there is no strongly connected component
7: for each vertex u ∈ G.V do
8: if u.inSCC = False then . Vertex u is not the part of any SCC
/* – – – – – Obtain SCC where vertex u is one of the vertex – – – – – */
9: L→ ← Obtain the set of vertices reachable from u (including u)
10: L← ← Obtain the set of vertices from where u can be reached (including u)
11: component ← L→ ∩ L← . SCC where vertex u is a member
12: SCComponents ← SCComponents ∪ {component} . Add the obtained SCC to the set of SCC
13: for each vertex v ∈ component do
14: v.inSCC ← True . Mark the vertices of SCC so that they do not take part again
15: end for
16: end if
17: end for
18: return SCComponents

9 Kruskal’s Algorithm
Algorithm 25 Kruskal’s Algorithm
Input: A connected undirected graph G = (V, E)
Output: Minimum weight spanning tree T of G
1: n ← |G.V | . Number of vertices in G
2: m ← |G.E| . Number of edges in G
3: T ← ∅ . Initialize minimum weight spanning tree
4: Sort the edges of G.E in non-decreasing order of their weight
5: for each vertex u ∈ G.V do
6: Make-Set(u) . Create a separate component for each vertex
7: end for
8: for each edge (u, v) ∈ G.E taken in non-decreasing order of their weight do
9: Repu ← Find-Set(u) . Find the component where u belongs
10: Repv ← Find-Set(v) . Find the component where v belongs
11: if Repu
6= Repv
then . u and v are from different component
12: T ← T ∪ {(u, v)} . Add edge (u, v) to the minimum weight spanning tree T
13: Union(Repu
, Repv
) . Connect u and v
14: else . u and v are from the same component
15: Do nothing . Connecting u and v will give a cycle
16: end if
17: end for
18: return T

12 Bellman-Ford Algorithm
• If the graph G = (V, E) contains no negative-weight cycles reachable from the source s, then for all v ∈ V ,
the shortest-path weight δ(s, v) remains well defined, even if it has a negative value.
• If the graph G = (V, E) contains a negative-weight cycle reachable from source s, however, shortest-path
weights are not well defined.
• No path from s to a vertex on the cycle can be a shortest path – we can always find a path with lower weight
by following the proposed “shortest” path and then traversing the negative-weight cycle.
• If there is a negative-weight cycle on some path from source s to v, we define δ(s, v) = −∞.
Algorithm 30 Bellman-Ford Algorithm
Input: A directed graph G = (V, E) and a source vertex s ∈ G.V
Output: Shortest distance between s to all other vertices
1: n ← |G.V | . Number of vertices in G
2: m ← |G.E| . Number of edges in G
3: for each vertex u ∈ G.V do
4: u.key ← ∞ . Length of the shortest path from source vertex s
5: u.π ← Nil
6: end for
7: s.key ← 0 . Shortest distance from source vertex to itself is 0
8: for i ← 1 to n − 1 do
9: for each edge (u, v) ∈ G.E do
10: if v.key > u.key + w(u, v) then . There exists a better path to reach v from s
which goes through u
11: v.key ← u.key + w(u, v)
12: v.π ← u . Shortest path to v has been explored through u
13: end if
14: end for
15: end for
/* – – – – – – – – Check for Negative weight cycle reachable from s – – – – – – – –*/
16: for each edge (u, v) ∈ G.E do
17: if v.key > u.key + w(u, v) then
18: return False . Negative weight cycle reachable from s
19: end if
20: end for
21: return True . No negative weight cycle reachable from s
